title: How Trust Grows in Ordinary Follow-Through
summary: Team trust rarely comes from big rescues. It grows from small promises kept, early heads-ups when dates slip and honest repair, with messages you can copy.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
10:15am, team channel: "Migration check done, no issues found. I'll attach the notes before lunch." Nobody replies. The thread scrolls on. At 11:50 the notes show up, in the ticket, where everyone expected them. Still no emoji party. But the next time this person says "before lunch," nobody on the team bothers to set a reminder to chase them.

That's how trust on an engineering team usually grows. One big rescue rarely does it. A long run of small, boring evidence does. Someone says they'll look at the failing test, and they do. Someone sees they'll miss a date and says so on Tuesday instead of Friday. Over time the team learns what each person's words are worth when things get busy.

Google found the same thing when it studied what made its teams effective. Project Aristotle looked at 180 teams (115 engineering teams and 65 sales teams) and named five dynamics that mattered. Psychological safety came first. Dependability came second, described as teammates who "reliably complete quality work on time." One of the survey questions they used to measure it is about as plain as it gets: "When my teammates say they'll do something, they follow through with it" (Google re:Work, Understand team effectiveness).

Small promises hold up other people's plans

Most of a team's day runs on promises so small nobody writes them down:

  • "I'll send you the link."
  • "I'll check the logs after standup."
  • "I'll ask design about the empty state."
  • "I'll add a test for that case."

Because they're small, it's easy to treat them casually. But someone else's plan is often sitting on top of each one. The designer is waiting on the answer to finish the spec. The reviewer is holding the approval until that test exists. When small promises get kept, coordination gets cheap: fewer reminders, fewer double-checks, fewer backup plans.

Distrust shows up as extra work

A missed small promise won't take production down. Repeat it a few times, though, and people start adding padding around you without saying so. They ask for proof earlier. They re-check things that shouldn't need re-checking. They start a parallel plan "just in case." None of this shows up on the board, and all of it costs hours. Low trust usually starts as coordination overhead that nobody puts a name to.

Don't let silence be the update

Follow-through doesn't mean never missing. Reliable people still hit surprise complexity, sick days, broken environments and priorities that change under them. What they don't do is go silent. They bring the bad news back to the team before anyone has to come looking for it, while there's still room to move the date or cut scope.

A good early update separates what you know, what you're estimating and what's still unknown. "Friday, if the API contract doesn't change" is far more useful than "Friday, guaranteed", because it tells people exactly what to watch.

An early heads-up that helps

"Heads-up on the export ticket: I said Wednesday, it's going to be Friday. The CSV library doesn't handle our date format, so I'm writing a small adapter. Known: the adapter is about a day. Unknown: whether the finance team needs the old column order. I've asked them and will update here by 3pm."

If you're stuck rather than just late, ask early. There's a whole post on why asking for help early is a skill.

Repair out loud

Everyone drops something eventually. What happens next matters more than the slip. Forgot? Say "I forgot, sending it now." Made the wrong call? Correct the record where people will see it. Someone waited on you? Name the cost and give a new date you can actually hit.

Google's SRE teams build this into incidents. Their postmortems are blameless: they "focus on identifying the contributing causes of the incident without indicting any individual or team", and they include follow-up actions to stop it happening again (Site Reliability Engineering, Postmortem Culture). Day-to-day repair works on a smaller scale with the same logic. Own it plainly, skip the drama, fix what's needed and move on.

A repair message

"My bad: I said I'd review your PR yesterday and didn't. I know that held up your merge. I'm on it now and you'll have comments within the hour."

What leaders choose to notice

Teams learn from what gets praised. If the only thing that earns a shout-out is the 2am rescue, people learn to perform urgency, and sometimes to let things get urgent. If leads also call out the boring wins (the early heads-up, the ticket closed with notes, the decision written down), people learn that steady, predictable work counts. You shouldn't need a crisis to find out who's dependable.

The most dependable teams aren't perfect. They're easy to read:

  • Every commitment has an owner.
  • Delays come with an early signal.
  • Decisions come with a short note.
  • Uncertainty gets said out loud, with a date for when it'll be resolved.

People can plan around each other because work doesn't vanish between meetings.

Try this week

  • Write down every small promise you make for three days. Count how many you closed without a reminder.
  • Next time a date slips, post the update the same day you know, using known, estimated and unknown.
  • When you drop something, send a one-line repair message before anyone asks.
  • In your next team meeting, thank someone for a boring, on-time piece of work by name.

Trust grows when your words still hold at the end of an ordinary day. One small promise, kept, tells the team they can build on it. Pick one this week and close it before anyone has to ask.

faqs.q: How do you build trust on an engineering team?
faqs.a: Mostly through small, repeated follow-through: doing what you said, by when you said it, and flagging early when you can't. Google's Project Aristotle, which studied 180 teams, named dependability as one of five dynamics of effective teams and measured it with the statement "When my teammates say they'll do something, they follow through with it."

faqs.q: What should I do when I'm going to miss a deadline?
faqs.a: Say so as soon as you know, and split the update into what's known, what's estimated and what's still unknown. "Friday, if the API contract doesn't change" helps people more than "Friday, guaranteed" because it tells them what to watch.

faqs.q: How do I recover trust after dropping something?
faqs.a: Repair it out loud and quickly: say what you missed, name the cost to the person who waited and give a new date you can actually hit. Google's SRE postmortems follow the same idea at incident scale: find contributing causes without blaming individuals, and attach follow-up actions.

faqs.q: How does low trust show up on a team?
faqs.a: As extra coordination nobody names: people ask for proof earlier, re-check work that shouldn't need it and keep backup plans just in case. None of it appears on the board, but it costs hours every week.
